author: TrentonBricken
text:
(assuming this is what separates us from all other species.)

To the extent deep learning is inferior (which seems to certainly still be the case) we may expect strong convergence up to this symbolic processing threshold but quick divergence afterwards?

author: TrentonBricken
text:
This is in the context of thinking how convergent we should expect deep learning to be with brains. 

Seems like human intelligence is obviously satisficing rather than maximizing for reproductive fitness. 

But only past the threshold of language ability/symbolic thought.

author: TrentonBricken
text:
For brains other limiting factors include: every other biological function; head size (for birth); social dynamics eg Elephant in the Brain (being unaware of your motives makes you better at deception). 

I’m defining intelligence loosely as the ability to solve problems.

author: TrentonBricken
text:
Photosynthesis is surprisingly  suboptimal at converting sunlight -> energy. Is this weak evidence for expecting brains to be suboptimal for intelligence? 

In both cases their function is a small part of the organisms entire utility function and often not the limiting factor.

text:
Our cognition is occurring at four different levels each with unique properties: genetic, synaptic, chemical, and environmental. The chemical level refers to extrasynaptic chemical gradients via volume transmission that I was unaware of (and I suspect others may be too).

6/10

author: TrentonBricken
text:
2. All cognition and our study of it should be action oriented and “embodied”. Cognition interfaces with our environment and ensures our survival through the production of action. There is no point in having senses if no action can be taken to respond to them. 

5/10

author: TrentonBricken
text:
Anderson reviews research showing that any specific brain region is involved in a large number of different cognitive operations. This is counter to our focus on modular localized cognition that fMRI emphasizes and has continued since the practice of phrenology.

4/10

author: TrentonBricken
text:
however, each region still contributes to many different functions just as a knife can be used to not only cut vegetables but also spread butter and tighten screws. 

3/10

author: TrentonBricken
text:
Rather than using the entire Spike protein that is 1273-AA long, we can hypothetically get even better population coverage with just a handful of epitopes of only between 8 and 25-AA long. Work showing these results: https://t.co/QXBTNhrZXy

21/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
However, that we could in the future accidentally encode additional viral proteins hidden inside our vaccines does give support to smaller, epitope based vaccine designs of the sort I have been previously involved in researching. 

20/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
Moreover, it is very important to emphasize that the FDA approved vaccines have been shown to be safe and so in this case there are not any problems with whether this novel gene is expressed or not.

19/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
However, the exact Spike nucleotide sequence for the ORF must be used for this novel gene to be encoded. We know Pfizer's vaccine is codon optimized in such a way that it does not encode this ORF and by proxy this novel gene. 

18/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
2. Note that Spike protein is used in all of our approved SARS-CoV-2 vaccines. For our DNA and mRNA based vaccines, encoding for Spike could also secretly encode for, and potentially express, this novel immune suppression gene. However...

17/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
There are two really cool things to me about this novel gene: 1. It is amazing just how optimized viruses are, simultaneously encoding Spike and a immune suppression gene (we know CoV-2 already does this in the N protein and ORF9b with leaky scanning h/t @_nathanrollins) 

16/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
Moving on to the discovery of the putative novel SARS-CoV-2 gene! It is inside the spike protein, 87-AA long and in a different reading frame. It is found to be highly conserved with the bat RatG13 sequence and have IRF3 and STAT suppression. 

15/n https://t.co/OMNcBiipCd

author: TrentonBricken
text:
A final assay uses flow cytometry and the NFkB pathway specifically to further investigate how it is affected by the different genes (these results support the findings of the first assay outlined). 

14/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
This successful infection by HSV-1 is indicated by fluorescence. This protocol and its results for the different coronaviruses are summarized: 

13/n https://t.co/NSF0vEIMva

author: TrentonBricken
text:
Both of these yeast cells are fused with a mammalian (HeLa) cell which will become infected *only* if the viral gene of interest is capable of immune suppression (see paper for more details for why/how).

12/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
The second assay takes a very different (and super cool) approach to identifying immune suppression genes. One yeast cell expresses the Herpes Simplex Virus-1 (HSV-1) genome. Another yeast cell expresses the viral gene of interest. 

11/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
Using this approach, we show for each gene across many different coronaviruses how much each suppresses the different transcription factors (in the heat-map red is reduced and green is increased translocation):

10/n https://t.co/gy1hLjjM0Q

author: TrentonBricken
text:
For example, in the left most column of this fig. IRF3 and NFkB fluoresce in the cytoplasm but not the nucleus. Upon stimulation, in the middle and right columns these transcription factors translocate making the nucleus light up and the cytoplasm darken.

9/n https://t.co/ZEXeVMStnT

author: TrentonBricken
text:
The first assay developed uses high throughput fluorescent microscopy to identify if a specific gene prevents translocation of the aforementioned transcription factors into the nucleus.

8/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
This figure shows highly simplified IRF3, STAT1 and NFkB pathways. All of these are transcription factors that translocate from the cytoplasm into the nucleus to express the proteins necessary to respond to infection.

7/n https://t.co/BZ6dmLujKm

author: TrentonBricken
text:
What are these immune responses? In humans, there are a number of intracellular signaling pathways responsible for detecting if the cell is infected. These pathways do things like tell the cell to kill itself (apoptosis) and warn other cells there is an infection.

6/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
For instance, SARS-CoV-2 is more transmissible and often has weaker symptoms than SARS-CoV-1 or MERS. This might be explained in part by greater immune suppression by SARS-CoV-2 genes.

5/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
Diving deeper into the paper: 

Viruses are cleared from the body unless they counteract the innate immune system. The degree of this counteraction may help us predict the transmissibility and pathogenicity of future viruses. 

4/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
3. A suite of high-content cell-based assays are introduced that can be used to rapidly characterize immune suppression of viral genes. These assays should be useful for pandemic responses and virology research more broadly.

3/n

author: TrentonBricken
text:
Key paper contributions: 
1. Many SARS-CoV-2 proteins are discovered to have enhanced immune suppression compared to other coronaviruses incl. SARS-CoV-1 and MERS. 
2. A potential gene is discovered overlapping the Spike gene that shows immune suppression capabilities.  

2/n
